draft.title: Rounding decimals
card: To round to a given number of decimal places, find the last digit you are keeping. Then look at the digit right after it.
If the next digit is 5 or more, round up: add 1 to the last digit you keep. If it is 4 or less, leave the last digit as it is. Then drop all the digits after it.
Example: round 3.476 to 1 decimal place. The last digit kept is 4. The next digit is 7, so round up. The answer is 3.5.
A rounded answer is an approximation. It is close to the exact value, but not equal to it. We write \(3.476 \approx 3.5\), using the approximately equal sign.
draft.remember: Look at the next digit: 5 or more rounds up, 4 or less stays. A rounded answer is an approximation, so use \(\approx\).

a.q: Round 6.382 to 2 decimal places. What is the answer?
a.why: The last digit kept is 8 and the next digit is 2. Since 2 is 4 or less, the 8 stays and the answer is 6.38. Rounding up to 6.39 looks at the wrong digit, as the 8 is not the digit that decides.
a.clue: Only the digit right after the last one you keep decides.

b.q: Mia rounds 7.8 and 4.1 to the nearest whole number to check that 31.98 is a reasonable answer to \(7.8 \times 4.1\). Which check is correct?
b.why: 7.8 rounds to 8 and 4.1 rounds to 4, so the estimate is \(8 \times 4 = 32\). The answer 31.98 is very close to 32, so it is reasonable. The check using \(7 \times 4\) reaches the right conclusion with a wrong estimate, because the 8 after the 7 means 7.8 rounds up.
b.clue: Round each number first, then compare the estimate with 31.98.

problems.detail: The card says a rounded answer is 'close to the exact value, but not equal to it'. That is not always true. For example, 6.380 rounded to 2 decimal places is 6.38, which equals the exact value. It should say it is usually or may not be equal.

The card only teaches rounding to a number of decimal places. It never teaches rounding to the nearest whole number, or using a rounded estimate to check whether an answer is reasonable. The question relies on both.

proposal.title: Rounding decimals
card: To round, find the last digit you are keeping and look at the digit right after it. If that digit is 5 or more, add 1 to the last digit kept. If it is 4 or less, leave it, then drop the rest.
Example: round 3.476 to 1 decimal place. The digit after the 4 is 7, so round up. The answer is 3.5.
If you round up a 9, it becomes 0 and you carry 1 to the digit on its left. So 5.97 to 1 decimal place is 6.0, and the 0 stays to show 1 decimal place.
A rounded answer is an approximation. It is close to the exact value, but it may not be equal to it. We write \(3.476 \approx 3.5\), using the approximately equal sign.
proposal.remember: Look at the next digit: 5 or more rounds up, 4 or less stays. A rounded answer is an approximation, so use \(\approx\).

a.q: Round 6.382 to 2 decimal places. What is the answer?
a.why: The last digit kept is 8 and the next digit is 2. Since 2 is 4 or less, the 8 stays and the answer is 6.38. Rounding up to 6.39 looks at the wrong digit, as the 8 is not the digit that decides.
a.clue: Only the digit right after the last one you keep decides.

b.q: A parcel weighs 4.598 kg. What is its mass rounded to 2 decimal places?
b.why: The last digit kept is 9 and the next digit is 8, so round up. The 9 becomes 0 and 1 carries to the 5, giving 4.60 kg. Writing 4.59 kg ignores the 8, and 4.510 kg adds 1 to the 9 without carrying.
b.clue: What happens when you add 1 to a 9?
